title: How Many Triangles Can You Build
statement:
`sides` lists the lengths of sticks. Count the **triples of different sticks** (different positions in the list) that can be the three sides of a triangle with a **positive area**: the sum of any two lengths must be **strictly greater** than the third.

Two triples are different if they use different positions, even when the lengths are equal.

examples.explanation: Valid: (3, 4, 6), (3, 6, 7) and (4, 6, 7). (3, 4, 7) fails because 3 + 4 = 7 is not greater than 7.

hints.nudge: For three lengths a <= b <= c only ONE of the three conditions can fail. Which one? That reduces the check to a single comparison.
hints.pattern: Sort the lengths. Fix the longest side c (by position, scanning from the end) and use two pointers on the part before it: if a + b > c, every stick between a's position and b's position works with b.
hints.pseudocode:
sort sides
count = 0
for k = n - 1 down to 2:
  i = 0; j = k - 1
  while i < j:
    if sides[i] + sides[j] > sides[k]: count += j - i; j -= 1
    else: i += 1
return count
hints.walkthrough: Testing all triples is O(n^3). After sorting, for a triple a <= b <= c the conditions a + c > b and b + c > a hold automatically (c is at least as long as b and a), so only a + b > c has to be checked. Fix the longest stick c at position k and look for pairs (i, j) with i < j < k and sides[i] + sides[j] > sides[k]. Put one pointer at the start (i) and one just before k (j). If sides[i] + sides[j] > c then every position from i to j - 1 also works together with j (they are at least as long as sides[i]), which gives j - i triangles; then move j left. Otherwise i is too short for j: move i right. Each k costs O(k), the total is O(n^2). Zero-length sticks never help because a + b > c needs c < a + b.
